description: Formed with the intention to innovate and resolve problems in present day
summary: Our project is a simulation that compares earth, moon and mars places that share different analogical characteristics like geography, temperature, topography, etc. Before you start the simulation you will be able to select between an earth place that has been already selected before because of its characteristics with a mars or moon place. Comparing their different characteristics and bien able to run a simulation of how a Rover would act differently in both earth and moon or mars and see what slopes to avoid and how much energy it uses. This will help scientists to not only look to the places and guess. But to really compare the data and find the best places in earth to test missions before the real missions.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Planetary Terrain Mapping is a web-based terramechanics and pathfinding engine that evaluates whether an Earth site, like the Salar de Uyuni, is a valid mobility analog for a planetary target such as Mars' Jezero Crater or the Moon's Shackleton Crater. It processes 60x60 Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) and applies Mohr-Coulomb soil physics—factoring in local gravity, internal friction angle, and soil cohesion—to calculate wheel slip and mark shear-failure hazards. With these physics established, the engine runs an 8-directional Min-Heap A* algorithm to navigate an articulated rover along the most energy-efficient, hazard-free route.

What benefits does it have?

The platform introduces Simultaneous Locked Constraints, allowing engineers to set rover specifications like maximum slope, energy cost, and grip just once while the engine instantly simulates traversal across both the Earth analog and the planetary target at the same time. By computing exact energy expenditure, path length, and hazards avoided, it outputs a quantitative Analog Similarity Score percentage that replaces subjective estimates with hard mathematical variance.

What is the intended impact of the project?

This tool directly reduces the immense financial and operational risks of planetary exploration. By mathematically proving that a terrestrial analog accurately mirrors the slip risks, steep slopes, and energy demands of Mars or the Moon, it ensures engineers are solving the correct physical problems before deploying multi-billion-dollar hardware to space.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The frontend and simulation engine were built using JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, and CSS3, utilizing the HTML Canvas API for 60-FPS real-time rendering. We used Python scripts to process raw topographical datasets into normalized JSON and CSV elevation matrices. The entire project was developed in Visual Studio Code on Windows and is hosted live via GitHub Pages.

How is your project creative?

The engine defies conventional single-map testing by utilizing a natively split-screen, dual-environment workspace that transforms highly complex geotechnical formulas into an accessible, color-coded thermal heatmap. Furthermore, animating a 6-wheel rover with a radar pulse and a live telemetry tag visually bridges the gap between raw mathematical data and practical mission control execution for non-technical stakeholders.

What factors did your team consider?

We carefully balanced scientific validity with usability, combining rigorous terramechanics—such as calculating slip penalties via exact Martian and Lunar gravity constants—with an intuitive UI where sliders control complex variables without requiring users to rewrite code. Because NASA datasets continuously evolve, we avoided strictly hardcoding maps and instead built a seamless data bridge that parses live JSON or CSV files from Python directly in the browser. Finally, we prioritized scalability by designing the engine to automatically normalize any incoming elevation array to fit the 60x60 grid, ensuring the platform is immediately ready to test any future planetary landing site.
